Case study

Carry: A Patient Experience Extension

An extension to an existing patient experience: prepare for a visit, then read the conversation back afterwards.

Role
Product designer — patient flow, states, visual language
Team
Three designers, inside a larger design organisation
Phase
MVP development began in Playground following stakeholder review
Outcome A conversation patients can read back

I took Carry from a workshop premise to a scoped MVP and into an initial Playground build. A leadership change stopped the work before release.

What I contributed

  • Turned the premise into an end-to-end patient flow.
  • Proposed the boundaries for AI-assisted content and designed the interface that holds them.
  • Designed the upload, transcription and failure states.
  • Surfaced tradeoffs with product and engineering before they became build cost.
Problem & Context Remembering a conversation you only get once

Proto personas

Built from onsite and Maze pilot behaviour and the feedback the team held. No interview study, no quotes.

Maya Patel, 42

Breast cancer treatment follow-up

Situation
In the follow-up period after treatment, where visits sit at set intervals and part of what each one decides is whether the interval changes. Maya arrives with one specific concern rather than a general one, which is the pattern the pilot kept showing: patients who came in with something particular went straight to writing questions.
What they carry into the appointment
A result whose meaning is not obvious from the number, something noticed since the last visit that may or may not belong in the conversation, and a question that has been rewritten more than once.
What they need afterward
The interval, and the reason for it. The date is the easy half to keep; the sentence that explained it is the half that goes.

Jordan Lee, 31

Kidney function monitoring

Situation
Monitoring is a sequence of numbers, so most visits are a comparison with the last one. Jordan is fluent in the vocabulary and less sure what a movement inside it means. Questions accumulate between appointments rather than arriving all at once.
What they carry into the appointment
The latest figure and the direction it moved, plus a list built across several weeks — mostly variations on what would have to change for the plan to change.
What they need afterward
Instructions to remember and follow-ups to complete before the next test, in the order they were actually given.

Alex Morgan, 36

Prenatal care appointment

Situation
Appointments are frequent and short, and each one adds instructions to the ones already given. Alex arrives with more to report than to ask — the other pilot pattern, where someone less certain what to ask browses suggestions instead of writing their own.
What they carry into the appointment
Symptoms noticed and half-forgotten since the last visit, and a sense of what is probably worth raising without much confidence about which parts are.
What they need afterward
What happens next, and which of the instructions belong to this week rather than to the last three appointments.

The complaint in the feedback the team held was rarely one forgotten fact. It was the whole fifteen minutes.

Carry had to be a layer on an existing patient product — identity, appointments and navigation were not mine — so I scoped it to the moment around the conversation.

Research & Direction What changed the direction

No interview study. I had the team’s premises and the feedback they held.

Patients kept refining questions, so editing is immediate and reversible. I ruled out generated answers, because patients need to verify what was said. Recording moved outside Carry, to avoid consent complexity.

Testing & Iteration Testing changed the order

A one-week onsite workshop with patients, and a parallel Maze study against the core mobile flows.

  1. Patient prototype
  2. In person ~3 unique patients a day in my sessions. Task-based moderated testing, observation, follow-up questions.
    Maze ~5–6 unique testers a day. Unmoderated task testing: completion, time on task, misclicks, heatmaps, comments.
  3. Behaviour patterns
  4. Design iteration
  5. Retest

Tasks tested

  1. T1Prepare for visit
  2. T2Add a question
  3. T3Reorder questions
  4. T4Upload recording
  5. T5Find what the doctor said
  • ~85–90%completed preparation unassisted, after iteration
  • ~20–35%faster to begin building a question list, after the sequence changed
  • ~80–90%found something the doctor said in a saved conversation
  • ~80–90%understood a matched answer came from the uploaded recording, after stronger source cues

Reconstructed ranges from onsite and Maze pilot testing. Exact historical Maze exports are not available.

Testing separated a usability problem from a difference in intent.

Version 1

Preparation checklist → My questions → Suggested questions

I had put logistics first. Patients with a specific concern went straight past the checklist.

  • ~70–80% completed the whole flow without help
  • ~20–30% hesitated, backtracked, or bypassed the checklist
  • Patients with a specific concern usually tried to reach question-building first
  • Patients less sure what to ask were more likely to browse suggestions

The checklist worked. Its position didn’t.

I changed the information hierarchy instead of redesigning a component patients already understood.

Version 2

My questions → Suggested questions → Preparation checklist

I changed the sequence rather than the component.

Version 1Version 2

  • ~85–90% completed preparation unassisted
  • ~20–35% faster entry into question-building
  • ~10–15% hesitation or unnecessary backtracking

Reconstructed pilot patterns. The sequence change is not the only thing that moved between rounds, and these do not prove it caused every improvement.

Finding an answer wasn’t enough

Patients reached an answer without knowing where it came from.

BeforeAfter

  • ~80–90% found something the doctor said in a saved conversation
  • ~80–90% understood the matched answer came from the recording, after stronger source cues

The second figure is source comprehension, not matching accuracy.

What changed

Design Priorities Clarity, Trust, Performance

The order the problems arrived in: clarity broke first, trust decided what the product would not do, performance was what was left.

Clarity

What I saw

Three kinds of content shared the pre-appointment screen and nothing looked like it belonged to the patient.

What I did

Suggestions became optional and reversible, editing moved into the row, and the row got a minimum height rather than a fixed one.

What changed

The list reads as the patient’s own.

Patients build their own list of questions.

Add a suggested question, then undo it.

Try it — add a suggested question, then undo it

Responsiveness across different devices

Patients write long questions, so the row grows. Same type, spacing, 56pt minimum row and 44pt targets on every device.

Edit the question text

Try it — type a longer question
Examples
Device

Trust

What I saw

The obvious next move was to let the model answer the questions. A patient cannot check a summary, and a wrong one could send someone into three months of surveillance.

What I did

The answer is a quotation, badged and editable, with a route to the moment it came from. Where nothing was said clearly enough to quote, the question stays visibly unanswered.

What changed

It cost the product its most demo-able feature, and it is the decision I would defend hardest.

Patients can see exactly what was said.

Open a transcript, or dismiss an answer.

Try it — open a transcript, or dismiss an answer

Patients choose what to upload.

The patient supplies the recording, so declining had to be a real option.

Try it — tap Upload recording

One conversation, whether it’s live or saved.

A record you can still edit is not a record, so the controls leave when it is saved.

Try switching between Active and Saved

Performance

What I saw

Upload, transcription and matching all take real time and all fail, and every one of those moments was a blank in my file.

What I did

Each failure is a state of the real component, answering three questions in order: what happened, what was kept, what to do next. I checked the recovery paths with engineering.

What changed

The flow became estimable.

It still makes sense when things go wrong.

Change a condition.

Everything working normally.

Design System One reference the team could build from

By the third flow I was redrawing the same row and getting it wrong a different way each time.

One interactive colour, one ink ramp, one divider. The teal has two values because it carries white type on light and near-black on dark.

What changed

Two other designers picked up screens from this without asking me what a row was supposed to do.

Reflection Where it landed

The flows, states and component set were defined and a Playground build had started when priorities changed above me.

What I would do differently

I would test the premises before drawing. Every assumption here is testable and none of them were tested first.

What I carry forward

The subtraction. Deciding early that Carry does not record, does not deliver results and does not let a model write anything removed most of the hard problems before they became design problems.

The design system, flows and seeded content are the project’s own. The prototypes are rebuilt here from that documentation, so they behave rather than being screenshots.

OptiFlow

Case study

OptiFlow

The moment a reviewer disagrees with a model, designed so the disagreement becomes feedback the system can learn from.

Role
Product designer — tagging stage, review flow
Team
Ops reviewers, product, engineering
Phase
Design delivered and handed to engineering
Outcome Human judgement in the loop

I designed the tagging stage: a reviewer accepts, corrects or adds to what the model proposed, and that judgement becomes feedback.

Measured accuracy was 99.5% at ingest and 99% at extraction. Tagging carried a 75% target the feedback loop was meant to move. I did not own the model, so these are context rather than my result.

What I owned

  • The tagging workspace and the accept / correct / add interaction
  • Model confidence and its evidence, at the moment of judgement
  • A required reason before a correction can be validated
  • States for low confidence, no suggestion and disagreement
  • What the feedback loop could realistically consume, with engineering
  • The stage kept on the existing component set
Problem & Context Corrections with no reasoning attached

Reviewers were correcting the model all day and none of it reached the model. The judgement evaporated.

The problem was the moment a person disagrees with a model. Accepting was easy and correcting was awkward, so the interface was teaching reviewers to accept.

Research & Direction What changed the direction

Every suggestion looked equally certain

Reviewers had no way to tell a confident suggestion from a guess. The confidence figure existed; the evidence behind it did not.

Engineering could only use categorised feedback

Free-text corrections were not something the loop could consume. That reframed the design: the reason had to be categorised at the point of correction.

Disagreement was being treated as an exception

So I designed disagreement as a first-class action rather than an exception.

  • System step
  • LLM reasoning
  • Human judgment
  • Feedback & refinement
1 / 16

optiSTREAM systemAutomated pipeline

Denial notice

optiSTREAM UIWhat the reviewer sees

ReviewerJudgment layer

Accept, remove or add a tag. A change opens the feedback panel, and Validate stays disabled until a reason is given.

optiSTREAM systemFeedback & refinement

Structure, terminology, examples, tags, confidence levels, justification reasons and accuracy figures are the project’s own. The diagrams are redrawn here.

Design Priorities Clarity, Trust, Performance

Clarity before a reviewer can decide anything, trust to stop them accepting on autopilot, performance because the step costs time somebody signs off.

Clarity

What I saw

The document, the suggested tag and the confidence figure sat in three places. Timing a reviewer against it made the cost obvious.

What I did

One place, fixed order: what the model proposed, how sure it is, what it read to get there, then the action.

What changed

The decision became a glance instead of a search.

Trust

What I saw

A reviewer who stops checking is worse than no model at all, and a fast Accept button is very good at producing one.

What I did

The evidence sits where a reviewer has to pass it to accept, and disagreeing carries the same weight as agreeing.

What changed

The feedback loop only produces anything if people are willing to use it.

Performance

What I saw

Requiring a reason is friction, and friction at volume is a cost somebody signs off. Ops were right to push back.

What I did

I made the reasons a short fixed list rather than free text: one tap, and the output is already categorised. Then I took the numbers to review.

What changed

The step survived review. Slower per correction, in exchange for the only feedback that could move the model.

Reflection Where it landed

I did not own the model, the pipeline or the release. What I owned was the stage where a person disagrees with a suggestion, and what that disagreement becomes.

What I would do differently

I would have instrumented the reason codes from day one. The whole design rests on reviewers picking an accurate reason under time pressure, and nothing in the build checks whether they do.

What I carry forward

Asking engineering what the system can consume before designing what the person does.

Structure, terminology, examples, tags, confidence levels and justification reasons are the project’s own. The diagrams and prototypes are rebuilt here.

Case study

Design System Audit

I audited a clinical portal against the decisions a provider makes in it, and rewrote the parts that were making them stop and interpret.

Role
Product designer — audit, component and copy standards, handoff
Team
Product, engineering, design system
Phase
Audit delivered as documentation and system rules
Outcome The library passed. The workflow did not.

The library was consistent. The workflows were not: the same required action appeared as a button, a link and a menu, and statuses named system states rather than whose move it was.

Contrast ratios are measured pairings from the audit, including one reported as it came out rather than corrected. Delivered as documentation and system rules, so there are no adoption figures here.

What I owned

  • Audited four workflows against the decisions inside them, not the library
  • Rewrote status and action copy to name an owner and a next step
  • Set how a next-step action ranks against the others in a row
  • Documented the colour system with a measured ratio behind every pairing
  • Defined the Provider Action Queue: one pattern for all four workflows
  • Wrote it as a build spec with states, approved copy and acceptance criteria
Problem & Context A library is not a workflow

A design system is normally audited against itself. That audit passes here, and the provider still cannot tell whose move it is.

So the unit of review was the workflow, not the component.

  • OrdersProviders review and complete test orders before submission. Status labels, table actions, submission errors
  • SpecimensProviders and lab teams track specimens through collection, transit, receipt, review and completion. Tracking states, timelines, ownership
  • ResultsProviders review results, sign off when needed, and access reports. Review states, alerts, report actions
  • TasksThe portal surfaces missing information, submission errors, clinical review and overdue work. Priority, required action, due dates
  1. Order created
  2. Specimen collected
  3. Lab reviews specimen
  4. Result generated
  5. Provider reviews result
  6. Task resolved

The question the audit asked of every screen

Can a provider quickly understand what is happening, what needs attention, and what action to take next?

What the Audit Found Three ways a row stopped saying whose move it was

Three things a work-queue row is made of: the action at the end, the status at the front, and what it says when something fails.

Actions had no rank

When the same action is a button in one row, a link in another and a menu in a third, the provider ranks the work instead of the interface.

Before Similar actions looked different across workflows

WorkflowStatusLast updatedAction
OrdersPending2h agoSubmit Order
ResultsReview4h agoOpen
SpecimensIn Progress1h agoDetails
TasksOpen30m ago…

After Every row exposes the next required action

WorkflowStatusRequired actionNext step
OrdersAwaiting provider actionConfirm order detailsReview order
ResultsNeeds clinical reviewReview and sign off on resultReview result
SpecimensLab review in progressTrack specimen progressView details
TasksSubmission errorAdd missing specimen sourceResolve issue

Labels now describe the provider’s task rather than the system’s operation, and the next step sits in the same column in every row.

System rule

Next-step actions take a distinct treatment per meaning — provider action, clinical review, detail, recovery, completion — and sit in the same column in every row.

Statuses left a question behind

The colour was already doing its job. Every status named a system state and left the provider holding a question about ownership.

  1. Who is it pending on?

    Pending→Awaiting provider action

    The provider owns the next step.

  2. Who needs to review it?

    Review→Needs clinical review

    Sign-off, not an inbox glance.

  3. What failed, and how do I fix it?

    Failed→Submission error

    Recoverable, so the provider expects a fix.

  4. Where is it in progress?

    In Progress→Lab review in progress

    The lab owns it; there is nothing to do.

  5. Was it delivered, reviewed, or closed?

    Complete→Results delivered

    Tied to a clinical outcome, not a workflow ending.

System rule

Status copy must clarify ownership, workflow state, and whether the provider needs to act.

Errors named a problem, not a fix

A failed submission stops a clinical test. The error states were visible; they did not say what to fix.

The status stops sounding final, the message names the field, and the action says what pressing it will do.

System rule

Every error carries four things: the error type, the specific cause, the recovery instruction, and an action-specific next step.

System Decisions One pattern, and colour that had to earn it

Rewriting labels fixes rows one at a time. Two decisions had to hold across all four workflows.

The Provider Action Queue

Four workflows ask the same question in four vocabularies, each answered with generic components.

  • Patient contextAppeared differently in every workflow. One structure, so work compares across all four.
  • Required actionSupporting details mixed IDs, test names and vague descriptions. A field that says what to do.
  • PriorityNot shown in workflow rows at all. A visible field.
  • Row structureEach workflow built its own. One pattern for all four.

Colour had to survive a dense table

Four of the five findings hand work to colour, in a dense table read at speed.

Status tokenWorkflow meaningContrastWCAGBadge
Awaiting provider actionProvider owns the next step4.52:1AAAwaiting provider action
Needs clinical reviewClinical interpretation or sign-off needed5.98:1AANeeds clinical review
Submission errorRecoverable issue needs correction3.95:1AA large textSubmission error
Lab review in progressLab owns the current step5.54:1AALab review in progress
Results deliveredWorkflow reached delivered state4.57:1AAResults delivered

Action tokens, measured the same way: provider action 6.24:1, clinical review 7.54:1, recovery 4.51:1, completion 5.11:1, informational outline 17.85:1. The border token is marked decoration only — the one value never allowed to carry a label.

  1. Status is never colour alone. Always paired with visible text, and with an icon on warning and error states.
  2. Semantic colour is used consistently. Orange is provider action, purple is clinical review, blue is a standard provider action, red is recoverable error, green is completion.
  3. Low-contrast values are decoration only. Borders and dividers need not meet text contrast, and must never carry a label or essential information.
  4. Red badge copy is handled carefully. Acceptable at badge size, not for small paragraph text, and always paired with an icon.
  5. New tokens are validated before use. Any new status, action or alert colour is checked for contrast before it enters the system.

System rule

Colour tokens are tied to workflow meaning rather than decoration, and no token carries meaning on its own.

Handoff & Reflection A screen is not an instruction

The inconsistencies were also appearing at handoff, where a static screen and a component example get read four different ways.

So the pattern was written as build instructions rather than drawn as a screen: behaviour and acceptance criteria for product, states and approved labels for engineering, and enough for an AI-assisted tool to build to.

Build spec

Provider Action Queue Row

Build ready

Purpose

Shows urgent provider work in a scan-friendly row with status, required action, owner, due date and next step.

Required fields

PriorityPatient / workflowStatusRequired actionOwnerDueNext step

Approved status copy

Awaiting provider action Needs clinical review Submission error Lab review in progress Results delivered Missing information

Action rules

  • Use task-specific labels.
  • Use “Review order,” “Review result,” “Resolve issue” or “View details.”
  • Do not use “Open,” “View,” “Done,” “Failed” or “Pending” in updated workflow tables.
  • Place the next step action in the far-right column.

Required states

DefaultHoverFocusSelectedLoadingEmptyErrorDisabledOverdue

Accessibility rules

  • Status must include visible text.
  • Do not rely on colour alone.
  • All actions must be keyboard accessible.
  • Focus states must be visible.
  • Error states must include recovery guidance.

Definition of done

  • The row includes all required fields.
  • The status uses approved design system copy.
  • The next step action appears in the far-right column.
  • The action label describes the task.
  • Error states explain what happened and how to recover.
  • Keyboard focus is visible.
  • Meaning remains clear without relying on colour.
  • The pattern works across orders, results, specimens and tasks.

What I would do differently

Standards are worth what gets adopted. I documented the rules and did not build the check somebody runs on a screen before it ships — every rule here is testable, and none of them were wired to anything that would catch a regression.

I also changed the words before I watched anybody read them. “Awaiting provider action” being clearer than “Pending” is an argument I made, not a result I measured.

What I carry forward

Auditing the workflow rather than the library. A component set can be perfectly consistent and still leave a provider unable to tell whose move it is.

Contrast ratios, token names, status copy, the build spec and the workflow examples are the audit’s own. The tables, badges and actions are rebuilt here as live components.
